argument: Robustness to norm-bounded or structured perturbations can require features different from those maximizing ordinary test accuracy. Under some distributions, no classifier simultaneously attains Bayes-optimal standard and robust risk, creating an explicit trade-off.
boundary: The trade-off depends on threat model, data distribution, representation, and available robust features.
Improved data or architecture can move the frontier.
Norm-bounded robustness may not correspond to semantic or physical perturbations.
claim: Robustness to norm-bounded or structured perturbations can require features different from those maximizing ordinary test accuracy. Under some distributions, no classifier simultaneously attains Bayes-optimal standard and robust risk, creating an explicit trade-off.
interpretation: A robustness claim is meaningless without threat model and attack budget. Principia should represent robustness as a scoped relation, not one global score.

argument: Allele-frequency change results from new variation, systematic fitness differences, finite-population sampling, migration, and recombination. Their relative strength depends on effective population size, selection coefficient, mutation rate, and population structure.
boundary: Simple models often assume random mating, constant fitness, and fixed population size.
Linked selection, demographic history, and spatial structure alter effective parameters.
Phenotypic evolution also depends on development and environment.
claim: Allele-frequency change results from new variation, systematic fitness differences, finite-population sampling, migration, and recombination. Their relative strength depends on effective population size, selection coefficient, mutation rate, and population structure.
interpretation: No single force should be inferred from a frequency trajectory without competing models. Large changes can arise from bottlenecks or migration rather than adaptation.
